sections.title: ML Systems as an Engineering Discipline

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Introduction and Chapter 1. Supplemental: Chip Huyen, Principles of Good Machine Learning Systems Design; Google Rules of Machine Learning.

This opening unit reframes machine learning as an engineering discipline rather than a model-building exercise. Students learn to describe an ML system as an interaction among data, model, infrastructure, objective, deployment context, and users. The key shift is that production ML fails differently from traditional software: behavior can degrade silently, data distributions move, labels arrive late, and success often depends on business, human, and operational constraints as much as accuracy. The unit introduces the AI Triangle, the ML lifecycle, and the five-pillar framework used throughout the course.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.

Studio: map one familiar AI product into data sources, model behavior, infrastructure, feedback loops, monitoring signals, and human stakeholders. Deliverable: a one-page system sketch with three likely failure modes.

sections.title: Deployment Paradigms and System Requirements

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Chapter 2. Supplemental: TinyML and edge AI materials from MLCommons and TensorFlow Lite.

This unit compares cloud, edge, mobile, TinyML, and hybrid deployments. Students learn that deployment is not a packaging detail; it is a design constraint that reshapes model size, latency budgets, privacy exposure, update cadence, power draw, connectivity assumptions, and operational responsibility. The unit uses a selection framework: start with the user context, quantify constraints, identify where data is produced, decide where inference should run, then plan how model updates and telemetry will move through the system.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.

Studio: select a deployment paradigm for three scenarios: hospital imaging triage, wake-word detection, and global recommendation ranking. Deliverable: a trade-off table covering latency, privacy, cost, power, update cadence, and reliability.

sections.title: Deep Learning Primer for Systems Engineers

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Chapter 3. Supplemental: open deep learning notes and framework tutorials for tensors, gradients, and inference pipelines.

This unit reviews deep learning from a systems perspective. The emphasis is not deriving every training rule from scratch, but understanding what computations happen, where memory is consumed, why batching matters, and how training and inference pipelines differ. Students connect tensors, layers, loss functions, gradients, optimizers, activations, preprocessing, and postprocessing to concrete system costs such as memory bandwidth, compute utilization, numerical precision, and data movement.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.
Studio: trace a small image classifier through preprocessing, forward pass, loss, backward pass, update, and inference. Deliverable: annotate each step with its main compute and memory pressure.

sections.title: DNN Architectures and Computational Patterns

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Chapter 4. Supplemental: FlashAttention and systems papers on transformer efficiency.

This unit studies architecture families as computational patterns. MLPs emphasize dense matrix operations, CNNs exploit spatial locality, RNNs process sequences recurrently, and transformers trade parallel sequence processing for expensive attention and memory behavior. Students learn to connect inductive bias to input structure, then connect architecture to system behavior: parameter count, activation memory, arithmetic intensity, data movement, batching shape, parallelization strategy, and hardware fit.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.
Studio: compare an MLP, CNN, RNN, and transformer for image, audio, time-series, and text workloads. Deliverable: architecture choice rationale with one system bottleneck for each.

sections.title: Security, Robustness, and Responsible AI

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Chapters 15, 16, and 17. Supplemental: NIST AI Risk Management Framework and robustness literature.

This unit brings together adversarial risk, robustness, reliability, fairness, accountability, documentation, and governance. Students study threat models, data poisoning, evasion, model extraction, privacy leakage, robustness testing, calibration, uncertainty, fairness metrics, human oversight, auditability, and risk management. Responsible AI is presented as an engineering requirement: systems need documented assumptions, measurable risks, monitoring, mitigation plans, and decision rights.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.

sections.title: Sustainable AI, AI for Good, Frontiers, and Final Design Review

content.value: Primary reading: Machine Learning Systems, Chapters 18 through Conclusion. Supplemental: sustainable AI talks, MLCommons materials, and course project review resources.

The final unit asks students to synthesize the full course. Sustainable AI connects efficiency to energy, carbon, hardware lifecycles, access, and organizational incentives. AI for Good requires more than intent: it requires stakeholder participation, problem fit, measurement, deployment realism, maintenance, and harm mitigation. The course closes with frontier systems such as foundation models and agentic systems, where scale, governance, evaluation, security, cost, and uncertainty interact. Students present a final ML system design with constraints, architecture, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, responsibility, and sustainability plans.
Supplemental sources for this unit are listed in the references below. Use them to compare the textbook framing with public talks, documentation, papers, and production guidance.

Studio: final design review. Deliverable: a 10-minute architecture presentation and a written systems brief covering requirements, data, model, infrastructure, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, risks, and sustainability.
